Depressed? Um... well, see, that’s the thing. I really wouldn't use the word depressed or down to describe it. And I’ve thought about this a lot, obviously, because of what I do for a living. 

When I think of being depressed, or when I see it in my clients at the clinic, it usually comes with this profound sense of sadness, right? Like a heaviness, or this crushing despair, or people find themselves crying all the time over things they can't even pinpoint. They feel miserable. But for me... no, I haven't been feeling sad or down like that at all. It’s not a dark cloud. It’s more like... well, like I was saying before, it's just an absence. 

If I actually felt sad, I think I would almost welcome it at this point, because at least sadness is a feeling. It means you're reacting to the world. Like when we had to move my relative in, maybe the normal reaction would have been to feel frustrated or overwhelmed, or maybe even a little sad about losing our privacy and our quiet space. But I didn't feel any of that. I just felt this creeping blankness. 

So, no, I'm not walking around feeling sorrowful or down most of the day. I’m just... neutral. But it's a very flat, empty kind of neutral. It’s exactly like I mentioned with my journaling—it’s not that I sit down and write about how terrible my life is or how hopeless I feel. I just don't write because there is absolutely nothing there to put on the page. The well is just dry. 

I actually tried explaining this to a colleague a few months ago, trying to put it into words without sounding like I was analyzing myself too much—because you know how we get in this field, we always try to analyze everything—but I had to make it clear to her that I'm not weeping in my car on the way to work. I don't feel like I've fallen into a pit. "Down" implies a direction, you know? It implies you've dropped below your baseline into sadness. But I haven't fallen anywhere. I'm just sort of... floating in this very gray, quiet space where nothing registers. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel depressed. Just unplugged.

Unusually high or energetic? Um... no, definitely not. And irritable? No, not that either. I mean, I know exactly what you're asking about—you're screening for mania or hypomania, right? I know we touched on this a moment ago when you asked about a history of depression, but just to be completely clear—because I know how crucial the timeline and previous diagnostic history are when you're trying to formulate a differential diagnosis—no, I have never had any prior episodes like this. And I've certainly never been diagnosed with or treated for depression in the past. 

It’s actually something I’ve been reflecting on quite a bit lately, trying to see if maybe I missed something in my own history. You know how it is in our field, sometimes we are the absolute worst at recognizing our own symptoms. We can spot a major depressive episode in a client from a mile away, but when it comes to ourselves, we rationalize it. We say, 'Oh, I'm just burned out,' or 'I'm just dealing with a heavy caseload.' So I really forced myself to look back, to comb through my twenties and thirties, my time in grad school, my early years working in community mental health—which, let me tell you, is a crucible that will test every coping mechanism you have. 

But even looking at it through that hyper-critical, clinical lens... there's just nothing there. I've never had a period where I felt this flat, this completely detached and empty. I've never been prescribed an SSRI, or an SNRI, or any kind of psychotropic medication for mood. I've never had to seek out therapy for depression. I mean, I've engaged in personal therapy, of course—I think anyone doing clinical social work needs to have their own therapist just to process the secondary trauma—but it was always focused on stress management, professional development, maybe some mild anxiety related to specific life transitions. It was never about treating a depressive episode. 

So, no, this current experience, this absolute void I've been living in for the past eight months... this is entirely unprecedented for me. There's no prior diagnosis, no prior treatment, no hidden history of depression that I'm just now uncovering. This is the first time my brain has ever done anything like this, which is probably why I feel so completely unmoored by it.
